Abstract 15 
Advances in spatially resolved transcriptomics provide unprecedented opportunities to 16 
characterise intercellular communication pathways. However, robust and computationally efficient 17 
incorporation of spatial information into intercellular communication inference remains 18 
challenging. Here, we present LARIS ( Ligand And Receptor Interaction analysis in Spatial 19 
transcriptomics), an accurate and scalable method that identifies cell type -specific and spatially 20 
restricted ligand-receptor (LR) interactions at single-cell or bead resolution. LARIS is compatible 21 
with all spatial transcriptomic technologies and quantifies specificity, infers sender -receiver 22 
directionality, and detects how differential interactions vary across time and space. To compare 23 
LARIS with existing methods, we established a simulation framework to generate ground truth of 24 
LR interactions with defined tissue architecture and gene expression patterns. LARIS 25 
demonstrates superior performances over other methods in accuracy and scalability. We further 26 
applied LARIS to human tonsil and developing mouse cortex spatial transcriptomics datasets 27 
collected from various spatial techniques. This uncovered the signalling mechanisms shaping 28 
tissue organisation and their changes over time. LARIS reveals cell type-, niche-, and condition-29 
specific signalling and scales to hundreds of thousands of cells in minutes. This provides an 30 
efficient and direct method for discovering the molecular interplay between apposed cells across 31 
development. 32 
Introduction 33 
Intercellular communication orchestrates tissue development, homeostasis, and responses to 34 
stress and disease 1. Computational inference of ligand -receptor (LR) interactions from 35 
transcriptomic data has therefore become a cornerstone for charting cellular interactions in 36 
complex tissues. However, computationally inference of cell -cell communication (CCC) faces 37 
challenges, including data sparsity, and spatial heterogeneity. Although recent advances in CCC 38 
algorithms have attempted to address some of these challenges by gene expression imputation 39 
and incorporating spatial constraints on LR interactions at populational level, they still struggle 40 
with low sensitivity and specificity, missing relevant interactions, producing many false -positive 41 
hits, respectively. Thus, sensitive, spatially resolved, and single -cell level reconstruction of 42 
intercellular communication networks remains a major unmet need1.  43 
 44 
To meet these needs, we introduce LARIS ( Ligand And Receptor Interaction analysis in Spatial 45 
transcriptomics) as an accurate method for LR interaction and CCC inference in spatial 46 
transcriptomic data. LARIS enhances the spatial interaction detection by combining in silico LR 47 
diffusion and local cellular heterogeneity via a spatial k-nearest neighbours (k-NN) graph, to infer 48 
single-cell level LR interaction scores and spatial specific CCC with cosine similarity. To rigorously 49 
compare our success with previous efforts, we also establish a spatial transcriptomics simulation 50 
framework that provides a reference ground truth for benchmarking CCC methods. We show that 51 
LARIS outperforms existing methods, accurately recovering spatial and cell type -specific 52 
interactions while maintaining low spatial false -positive rates. We further demonstrate the 53 
capabilities of LARIS in two case studies: (i) a human tonsil Slide -tags dataset2, where LARIS 54 
resolves niche - and cell -state-specific communication and recovers both known and novel 55 
signals; and (ii) a developing mouse cerebral cortex Stereo-seq dataset3–5, where LARIS identifies 56

Results 61 
 62 
Overview of LARIS 63 
LARIS is designed to identify and characterize LR interactions from spatial transcriptomics data 64 
using known databases and is compatible with both single -cell and bead/spot -based spatial 65 
datasets, enabling the discovery of cellular communication across diverse platforms (Fig. 1a and 66 
Extended Data Fig. 1). To improve both sensitivity and specificity, LARIS uses interaction 67 
abundance and cosine similarity to identify biologically relevant interactions, and a spatial k-NN 68 
graph to ensure that only spatially proximal cells are identified as interacting. 69 
 70 
LARIS begins by constructing a k-NN graph weighted by the physical distance between cells or 71 
spots (Fig. 1b). Using this spatial graph, the normalized ligand and receptor expression values 72 
are spatially diffused, modelling the local availability of each (Fig. 1c). An LR interaction score is 73 
then calculated for each cell or spot by element -wise product (i.e., Hadamard product) of the 74 
diffused ligand and receptor expression (Fig. 1d). To prevent diffusion artifacts from generating 75 
false-positive interactions, this score is set to zero if the cell or spot did not express either the 76 
ligand or the receptor in the original gene expression data. This scoring at the individual -cell or 77 
spot level increases sensitivity for interactions involving rare cell types and reveals communication 78 
patterns within subpopulations that are otherwise obscured by cluster -level or aggregated 79 
methods (e.g., CellChat6 and CellPhoneDB7). 80 
 81 
Building on these LR scores at single-cell/spot resolution, LARIS provides three complementary 82 
analytic approaches to discover the most specific interactions. First, LARIS identifies LR 83 
interactions with strong spatial patterns (Fig. 1e) using a cell type -agonistic approach. LARIS 84 
computes the cosine similarity between the calculated LR interaction scores and a spatially 85 
diffused version of those same scores. Building on the idea of negative sampling in network 86 
representation learning8, this observed similarity score is then corrected against a null value 87 
derived from spatially shuffled data. This yields a final spatial -specificity score for each LR pair 88 
(see Methods), of which the higher value indicates a stronger spatially localized pattern. 89 
 90 
Second, LARIS infers communication directionality between sender and receiver cell types (Fig. 91 
1f). To achieve this, it quantifies: (i) the cell-type specificity of ligand and receptor expression, (ii) 92 
the abundance of each LR pair for every cell type pairing, and (iii) a neighbourhood-enrichment 93 
score to detect co-localizing interactions between cell types. Combining this information with the 94 
LR spatial-specificity score yields a score for each LR pair in each sender-receiver cell type pair, 95 
which enables further prioritization of LR interactions based on cell types of interest and analysis 96 
of cell type communication patterns. 97 
 98 
Third, LARIS identifies differentially active interactions among different conditions or contexts, 99 
such as predefined tissue regions/niches, developmental stages or disease progressions (Fig. 100

Benchmarking on simulated data 110 
 111 
Prior work has highlighted low concordance among CCC methods, with major differences in top-112 
ranked predictions9. These discrepancies stem from divergent LR databases, the inclusion of 113 
interactions lacking experimental validation, and distinct model architectures 1,9. A persistent 114 
challenge in the field has been the benchmarking of these tools, which is hampered by the 115 
absence of comprehensive experimentally validated ground-truth datasets. 116 
 117 
To address this gap, we designed a simulation framework to generate spatial transcriptomics data 118 
with real-world tissue characteristics and known ground-truth LR interactions, providing full control 119 
over cell locations, gene expression (including genes that encode ligands and receptors), and 120 
active LR pairs with different levels of spatial and cell type specificities (Fig. 2a). This methodology 121 
enables rigorous, quantitative performance comparisons. 122 
 123 
The workflow first simulates scRNA -seq data using Splatter 10,11. Simulation parameters were 124 
calibrated to ensure that cell type identities are distinct and that quality metrics—such as dropout 125 
rates, unique molecule identifier (UMI) distributions, and gene variance —closely mimic those of 126 
a real-world reference, a human tonsil Slide -tags single nuclei RNA -seq dataset2 (Fig. 2b and 127 
Extended Data Fig.2). Next, these simulated cells are mapped onto complex spatial structures, 128 
which are generated either de novo using scCube12 or by templating from real tissue architectures, 129 
including mouse lung, small intestine, and developing brainstem, hair follicle and lymph node (Fig. 130 
2c, d). 131 
 132 
To establish a ranked ground truth, we defined an interaction's importance based on its 133 
expression specificity and spatial likelihood. First, we computed a 'relevance score' for each ligand 134 
and receptor in different cell types based on the simulation parameters that account for its 135 
simulated expression abundance and cell -type specificity (Extended Data Fig.3; see Methods). 136 
The ground -truth LR interaction ranking was then generated by multiplying these ligand and 137 
receptor relevance scores across all cell-type pairings. This comprehensive list was subsequently 138 
filtered for spatial feasibility, resulting in a final, ranked set of active LR interactions with varying 139 
specificities, known to occur between spatially proximal cell types (Fig. 2e, f). 140 
 141

including CellChat (non-spatial)13, CellChat-spatial (v2)6, and NICHES14. First, we assessed the 143 
efficiency of each method in prioritizing the top ranked ground -truth LR interactions. We plotted 144

We next tested LARIS’s ability to profile cellular communications on the human tonsil Slide -tags 169

LARIS identifies region and time specific interactions in the developing mouse brain 245 
 246 
We next applied LARIS to map the spatiotemporal dynamics of LR interactions during mouse 247 
brain development, a process governed by spatially organized signalling cascades42. We focused 248 
on the cerebral cortex, a structure defined by its distinct layered architecture and corresponding 249 
functional and transcriptional heterogeneity43. 250 
 251 
To assess this we applied LARIS to Stereo -seq datasets collected at different developmental 252 
stages of the mouse brain, i.e., embryonic day (E)14.5, E16.5, postnatal day (P)7, P14, and P773–253 
5 (Fig. 4a and Extended Data Fig. 5a). We annotated the cortex as upper and deep layers for the 254 
postnatal samples, and for the prenatal samples we included additional developmental cell types 255 
(Fig. 4a). 256 
 257 
LARIS identified differentially enriched spatial LR interactions across mouse cortex development. 258 
For example, the Slit1::Robo1 interaction, known to modulates proliferation and neurogenesis44,45, 259 
axon guidance and neuronal migration 46,47, was restricted to upper layer neurons prenatally but 260 
present in both upper and deep layer postnatally (Fig. 4b). Another intriguing example, the 261 
Sema3c::Plxna4 interaction, which was most prominent in the migrating and deep layer neurons 262 
prenatally, yet only sporadically present in the postnatal cortex (Fig. 4b). Sema3a, a closely 263 
related ligand with similar structure and expression to Sema3c, regulates interneuron positioning 264 
via Plxna448. By contrast, the role of Sema3c in the developing mouse cortex remains unknown, 265 
raising the possibility of a Sema3c::Plxna4 signalling axis. 266

Discussion 297 
 298 
Here we presented LARIS, a computational tool that allows the quantification of cell type and 299 
spatial LR interactions across time and space. We established a simulation -based ground-truth 300 
framework to measure and quantify its performance and demonstrated LARIS’s superior 301 
performance over existing methods. Applied to a human tonsil Slide -tags dataset, LARIS 302 
recovered canonical interactions underlying tissue organisation, cell migration, and immune 303 
responses, revealed previously unrecognised ligand sources, and separated cell states based on 304 
LR interaction patterns. In a Stereo -seq series of the developing mouse brain, LARIS resolved 305 
the spatial dynamics of LR interactions across cortical layers over multiple time points and linked 306 
these patterns to pathways central to brain development. 307 
 308 
Computational inferences of cell -cell interactions are powerful for hypothesis generation but 309 
ultimately require experimental validation to establish mechanism. Incorporating spatial context 310 
reduces predicted false positives; however, co -localisation (even physical proximity) does not 311 
ensure a functional effect on receiver cells because other mechanisms might mask or 312 
complement active signalling through parallel signals. A further limitation is that transcriptomics 313 
measures mRNA, whereas proteins (and their post -translational modifications) drive signalling. 314 
Coupling to proteomic assays and integrating chromatin accessibility (e.g., ATAC-seq) to read out 315 
responses in receiver cells will strengthen causal interpretation. 316 
 317 
Our benchmarking framework was designed to mimic real -world datasets and prioritise the 318 
reliable recovery of ligand-receptor (LR) pairs. A current limitation is that it does not directly assess 319

an invaluable reference for robustly evaluating such downstream predictions. 326

Many interactions involve co-receptors or multimeric ligands that act as complexes. LARIS does 328 
not yet model complex stoichiometry explicitly, which is an avenue for improvement. Given the 329 
zero-inflated nature of spatial assays, naively requiring all subunits to be co -detected would 330 
discard biologically plausible events lost to dropout and increase noise. Probabilistic complex 331 
scoring or partial-evidence models may offer a better balance between specificity and sensitivity. 332 
 333 
We have demonstrated that LARIS can comparatively analyse and quantify interactions across 334 
time points; it could likewise be used to contrast signalling between conditions and matched 335 
controls, enabling differential LR communication analyses. 336 
 337 
New spatial technologies are being developed constantly, and the field is moving towards the 338 
spatial profiling of cells compared to just dissociated single-cell data. LARIS will be an ideal tool 339 
to uncover and disentangle the hidden information inside the data and to point the most relevant 340 
focuses for future experimental planning. As the field moves towards better resolution and wider 341 
gene coverage, LARIS will likely be able to identify the most relevant ligand and receptors in the 342 
profiled sample and be ideal to analyse and quantify interactions across time and space. 343

Identification of niche enrichment of interactions 563 
To detect LR interactions that are enriched in functional regions or niches independent of cell 564 
type, we first assign regional labels to cells (e.g., cortical upper vs. deep layers). Because the LR 565 
integration score is defined per cell, standard single -cell differential frameworks can be applied 566 
directly: we compare per-cell LR scores across regions to identify interactions that are regionally 567 
differentially expressed. In practice, we treat each LR pair as a feature (gene) and perform 568 
differential testing across the region groups (e.g., marker -identification/rank-based tests with 569 
multiple-testing correction), potentially reporting effect sizes and region -wise prevalence. This 570 
yields a list of region -specific LR interactions that reflect spatially localized signaling programs 571 
without relying on cell type annotations; if desired, the same analysis can be repeated within cell 572 
type strata to differentiate regional effects per cell type. 573
